pos: n. (proper name; the third of the ten sons of Haman)
etymology: Persian, of uncertain meaning; proposed readings connect the name with aspa, a horse, a common element in Old Persian names. Nothing in the text settles it.
biblical_def: Aspatha is named once, in the roll of Haman's sons slain at Shushan: “And Parshandatha, and Dalphon, and Aspatha” (Esther 9:7). Ten names are given in three verses, and then the single sentence that interprets them: “The ten sons of Haman the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews, slew they; but on the spoil laid they not their hand” (Esther 9:10). Haman had plotted the destruction of a whole people and had built a gallows for one man; the decree he obtained for others fell on him, and his house with him. The king's own letter had said it plainly: his wicked device “should return upon his own head” (Esther 9:25). That is the law of the book of Esther, and the book never names God while demonstrating it on every page. Aspatha is one of ten names that exist in Scripture to show the recoil of a plot. The dictionary notes also what the Jews did not do: they did not touch the spoil, though the decree permitted it. Judgment executed, plunder refused — the restraint is recorded three times in the chapter, because deliverance is not a licence to loot.

corruption_summary: Esther 9 is read as vengeful excess; the chapter records a decree turned back on its author and plunder deliberately refused.
corruption_paragraphs: The slaughter at the end of Esther is the most commonly criticised passage in the book, read as a nationalist revenge fantasy. The text is more careful than its critics. The Jews acted under a royal decree, on a single appointed day, against those who sought their lives; and three times the narrator notes that they took no spoil, although the decree had granted it. A revenge fantasy does not legislate its own restraint.

The principle to recover is the justice of retribution that recoils on the plotter. Haman built a gallows and hanged on it; he obtained a decree and died by it; he had ten sons and they fell with his house. “Surely the wrath of man shall praise thee: the remainder of wrath shalt thou restrain” (Psalm 76:10). God is not named in Esther and governs every line of it.

pos: n. (proper name; the second of the ten sons of Haman)
etymology: Persian, of uncertain meaning; a connection with a root for sleeplessness or for dripping has been suggested, but nothing in the text decides it.
biblical_def: Dalphon is named once: “And Parshandatha, and Dalphon, and Aspatha” (Esther 9:7). He is the second of Haman's ten sons, and the whole of his existence in Scripture is his place in that list. The ten are worth a reader's thought, because they are the unintended consequence of their father's ambition. Haman had been promoted above all the princes (Esther 3:1) and set out to destroy a nation because one man would not bow; he died on his own gallows, and his sons died in the reckoning that followed. Children suffer for a father's wickedness in this world — not by being charged with his guilt before God, for “the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father” (Ezekiel 18:20), but by inheriting the ruin he built. The two truths sit together without strain: God judges each soul for its own sin, and a man's household reaps what he sows. Dalphon stands in the list as a warning to every father about what his ambition may cost the people in his house.

corruption_summary: Inherited consequence is confused with inherited guilt; Scripture distinguishes the two and holds both plainly.
corruption_paragraphs: The fall of Haman's sons is often urged as evidence that the Bible punishes children for parents, in contradiction of its own law. The contradiction is imaginary because the two things are different. Ezekiel 18:20 governs guilt before God: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father. Esther 9 records consequence in this world, where a house built on a plot falls when the plot does.

The principle to recover is that sin is never private. A man's wickedness reaches his table, his children, and his children's standing, and it reaches them without transferring his guilt to them. Fathers who think their ambitions concern only themselves should read the roll of Haman's sons, every one of them a name and nothing more, undone by a quarrel their father picked.

pos: n. (proper name; first-named of the seven princes of Persia and Media)
etymology: Persian, of uncertain meaning. The name heads a list of seven court names, all Persian, all appearing once, and all of doubtful derivation.
biblical_def: Carshena is named once, first of the inner council: “And the next unto him was Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, the seven princes of Persia and Media, which saw the king's face, and which sat the first in the kingdom” (Esther 1:14). These are the men Ahasuerus consulted when Vashti refused to come. To see the king's face was the highest privilege of the Persian court, and these seven had it. What they did with it is the point of the scene. The king, drunk and humiliated, asked what should be done, and Memucan answered with a counsel of state: let a royal commandment go out, unalterable among the laws of the Persians and the Medes, that Vashti come no more before the king (Esther 1:19). So the queenship fell vacant — which is how Esther came to the throne, and how a Jewish girl was in position when the decree of extermination was signed. Seven princes advising a furious king about a banquet were, without knowing it, preparing the deliverance of their empire's Jews. “The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD” (Proverbs 21:1), and so is his privy council.

corruption_paragraphs: Esther 1 is widely treated as colourful court anecdote, or as a late novella with no bearing on anything. Read as the book intends, it is the hinge. A drunken banquet, a queen's refusal, seven princes with a legal remedy, and an irrevocable decree together empty a throne that a Jewish orphan will occupy before the real crisis arrives.

The principle to recover is providence working through ordinary and even sordid causes. God is nowhere named in the chapter and is everywhere in it. “Who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (Esther 4:14) is a question that reaches all the way back to Carshena and his colleagues advising a furious king about a wife who would not come.

pos: n. (proper name; the seventh of the chamberlains of Ahasuerus)
etymology: Persian, of uncertain meaning. The Authorized Version's margin at Esther 1:10 glosses chamberlains as eunuchs, which is what the Hebrew term denotes in the Persian court setting.
biblical_def: Carcas is named once, last of seven: “On the seventh day, when the heart of the king was merry with wine, he commanded Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, and Abagtha, Zethar, and Carcas, the seven chamberlains that served in the presence of Ahasuerus the king” (Esther 1:10). They were sent to fetch Vashti, and she refused to come, and the empire's law machinery turned over as a result. The seven are court servants, named with the precision of a palace register and then dropped. Yet one of them is heard of again: Harbona, third in this list, is the chamberlain who at the critical moment told the king that Haman's gallows stood ready in Haman's own courtyard, and Haman hanged on it within the hour. A servant's word placed the rope. The dictionary draws from Carcas and his fellows the lesson the book teaches throughout: there are no small parts in providence. Seven eunuchs carrying a summons to a banquet set in motion the chain that saved a nation, and not one of them knew what he was carrying.

corruption_paragraphs: Court lists are easy to skip, and the seven chamberlains of Esther 1 are usually read as scene-setting. But the book brings one of them back at its turning point: Harbonah speaks a single sentence about a gallows and Haman is hanged on it. The register is not furniture; it is the cast.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God works His purposes through people who hold no office worth recording. Seven servants, a refused summons, a vacant throne, a chamberlain's remark — and a nation lives. No Christian in an obscure place has grounds to think his obedience is too small to matter.

pos: n. (proper name; the fourth of the chamberlains of Ahasuerus)
etymology: Persian, of uncertain meaning. The name resembles Bigthan (or Bigthana), the chamberlain who later conspired against the king, but Scripture distinguishes the two men.
biblical_def: Bigtha is named once, fourth in the list of chamberlains sent to fetch the queen: “he commanded Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, and Abagtha, Zethar, and Carcas, the seven chamberlains that served in the presence of Ahasuerus the king” (Esther 1:10). His name is close to that of Bigthan, one of the two doorkeepers who afterward sought to lay hands on Ahasuerus and whose plot Mordecai overheard and reported (Esther 2:21-22). The dictionary keeps them distinct: the text names them separately, in different offices, in different chapters. The near-identity of the names is a reminder of how crowded and how perilous that court was. Palace service in Persia meant proximity to absolute power with no security whatever — one chamberlain carries a summons, two others plot a murder and are hanged for it, and the record of that hanging, written in the king's chronicles and read aloud on a sleepless night, is what saved Mordecai and ruined Haman. Even the registry of a court conspiracy was an instrument in God's hand.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the providential use of records. A sleepless king, a book of chronicles read aloud, an old entry about a foiled plot — and the whole plan of Haman unravels. pos: n. (proper name; the second of the chamberlains of Ahasuerus)
etymology: Persian, of uncertain meaning; a connection with a word for a eunuch or for booty has been proposed without proof.
biblical_def: Biztha is named once, second in the roll of chamberlains: “he commanded Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, and Abagtha, Zethar, and Carcas, the seven chamberlains that served in the presence of Ahasuerus the king” (Esther 1:10). The errand they were given was to bring Vashti to be displayed before a hall of drunken men at the end of a seven-day feast, and she would not come. The book records the king's fury and the council's remedy without pausing to praise or blame the queen, and the dictionary will not supply a verdict the text withholds. What it will mark is the setting. This was a court where a wife was summoned as an ornament, where seven servants carried the command, and where refusal cost a crown. Scripture describes such a world with unflinching plainness and without approving it. The honour the Bible requires between husband and wife — the husband giving honour to the wife, dwelling with her according to knowledge (1 Peter 3:7) — is nowhere in Esther 1, and the chapter is the better witness for not pretending otherwise.

corruption_paragraphs: Esther 1 is regularly cited as evidence that the Bible approves of treating wives as property, since it narrates exactly that. The inference confuses description with prescription. The chapter reports a drunken king, a woman summoned for display, and an irrevocable law passed in anger; it commends none of it, and the reader who wants the Bible's doctrine of marriage must go to the texts that teach it.

The principle to recover is that the husband's headship is a charge to honour, not a licence to use. “Dwell with them according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife” (1 Peter 3:7), with the sanction attached that a man's prayers are hindered otherwise. Ahasuerus had the power of an empire over one woman and used it as a heathen; the standard for a Christian husband is Christ, who gave Himself.

pos: n. (proper name; a correspondent who wrote against Jerusalem to Artaxerxes)
etymology: Of uncertain derivation; the Authorized Version's margin at Ezra 4:7 offers the alternative rendering in peace, taking the word as a phrase rather than a personal name.
biblical_def: Bishlam is named once: “And in the days of Artaxerxes wrote Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel, and the rest of their companions, unto Artaxerxes king of Persia; and the writing of the letter was written in the Syrian tongue, and interpreted in the Syrian tongue” (Ezra 4:7). The margin notes that the word may be read in peace rather than as a name, and the dictionary records the uncertainty plainly rather than resolving it by preference. Either way the verse is the opening of a campaign conducted entirely on paper. The enemies of the returned exiles did not besiege Jerusalem; they wrote letters. Three successive Persian reigns received petitions arguing that the city was seditious by history and would withhold tribute if rebuilt, and the letters worked: “Then ceased the work of the house of God which is at Jerusalem” (Ezra 4:24). A lie in the right chancery stopped the temple for years where no army had. The devil's most effective instruments against the church have more often been documents than swords, and Ezra 4 is the chapter that says so.

corruption_summary: Opposition to the church is pictured as persecution by force; Ezra 4 shows it chiefly as paperwork and accusation.
corruption_paragraphs: Hostility to God's people is imagined mostly in terms of violence, which makes the quieter forms hard to recognise. Ezra 4 is a chapter of letters. The adversaries gather signatures, frame the city as historically rebellious, appeal to the king's revenue, and secure an order that halts the temple for years. Not a sword is drawn and the work stops.

The principle to recover is that God's eye outlasts the chancery. “But the eye of their God was upon the elders of the Jews, that they could not cause them to cease” (Ezra 5:5). The same empire whose officials stopped the building later financed it, and the Chronicler credits the finishing to the commandment of the God of Israel first and the Persian kings second. Paper can delay the house of God; it cannot cancel the decree behind it.

pos: n. (proper name; an Assyrian king who resettled peoples in Samaria)
etymology: Aramaic 'Osnappar, generally identified with the Assyrian royal name borne by Esarhaddon's successor. The Authorized Version styles him the great and noble Asnappar, following the Aramaic of the letter.
biblical_def: Asnappar is named once, and the naming is a quotation: the adversaries of Judah, writing to Artaxerxes, describe themselves as “the rest of the nations whom the great and noble Asnappar brought over, and set in the cities of Samaria” (Ezra 4:10). The honorifics are theirs, not Scripture's. These are the peoples Assyria transplanted into the northern kingdom after it carried Israel away — the mixed population whose descendants became the Samaritans — and in their letter they cite the king who deported them as a mark of standing. There is a deep irony in it. They boast of the man who uprooted them, and they write to a later empire to prevent the rebuilding of a temple belonging to the people whose land they had been given. Assyria's policy of mass resettlement was itself the LORD's judgment on Israel's idolatry, executed by a king who knew nothing of Him: “he doeth according to his will in the army of heaven, and among the inhabitants of the earth” (Daniel 4:35). Asnappar moved nations like furniture and was himself furniture in the hand of God.

corruption_summary: Imperial population transfer is read as politics only; Scripture names Assyria the rod of God's anger and holds the rod accountable.
corruption_paragraphs: The Assyrian deportations are standardly explained in terms of imperial management, and so they were. Scripture adds the governing cause and does not let it go: “O Assyrian, the rod of mine anger” (Isaiah 10:5). Israel's exile was the LORD's judgment on her idolatry, carried out by a king pursuing his own policy, and the same chapter of Isaiah goes on to sentence the rod for its arrogance.

The principle to recover is that God uses wicked powers without excusing them. Asnappar is a divine instrument and a guilty man at once, and the letter that calls him great and noble is written by people being used in their turn. “None can stay his hand, or say unto him, What doest thou?” (Daniel 4:35) is the only sane posture before a God who governs empires that do not know Him.

pos: n. (proper name; a people or an official class in the Persian administration west of Euphrates)
etymology: Aramaic 'Apharsekaye, of uncertain reference. Whether an ethnic group or a title of office (envoys, or officials of a particular rank) is intended cannot be determined from the text.
biblical_def: The Apharsachites appear twice, both times as companions of the Persian governor beyond the river: “The copy of the letter that Tatnai, governor on this side the river, and Shetharboznai, and his companions the Apharsachites, which were on this side the river, sent unto Darius the king” (Ezra 5:6), and in Darius's reply, “Now therefore, Tatnai, governor beyond the river, Shetharboznai, and your companions the Apharsachites, which are beyond the river, be ye far from thence” (Ezra 6:6). They came to Jerusalem, found the elders building, and asked by what authority — and here the account turns remarkable. Instead of stopping the work on their own authority, they wrote to Darius and asked that the archives be searched. The archives were searched; the decree of Cyrus was found; and Darius ordered not only that the building proceed but that the royal treasury pay for it. The investigation intended to halt the temple financed it. “But the eye of their God was upon the elders of the Jews, that they could not cause them to cease” (Ezra 5:5). Officials doing their duty honestly became the means by which the house was finished.

corruption_summary: Pagan officialdom is assumed uniformly hostile; here an honest inquiry became the means of the temple's funding.
corruption_paragraphs: It is easy to read every Gentile authority in Ezra as an enemy, but the book does not permit it. Tatnai and the Apharsachites asked their question, reported the answer they were given, and requested a search of the records rather than issuing a stop order. Their correctness was the instrument of the temple's completion and of a royal grant toward its cost.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God governs the machinery of unbelieving states for His church's good. An archive in Babylon held a decree that a Persian king honoured and paid out on. Christians under hostile or indifferent government may pray for exactly this and expect it, because the eye of their God is upon them while the letters travel.

pos: n. (proper name; one of the peoples resettled in Samaria, named in a letter against Jerusalem)
etymology: Aramaic Dehaye, of uncertain reference; a connection with the Dahae, a people east of the Caspian known to classical writers, has been proposed without proof.
biblical_def: The Dehavites are named once, in a roll of signatories: “Then wrote Rehum the chancellor, and Shimshai the scribe, and the rest of their companions; the Dinaites, the Apharsathchites, the Tarpelites, the Apharsites, the Archevites, the Babylonians, the Susanchites, the Dehavites, and the Elamites” (Ezra 4:9). Nine peoples are listed, and the point of listing them is weight. This is a petition got up with as many names behind it as could be gathered, and the letter it introduces is a model of effective slander: Jerusalem is called a rebellious and bad city, the king is warned that his revenue will suffer, and he is invited to search the records and see for himself. The accusation was answered and the work stopped. What the Dehavites and their eight co-signatories prove is that a coalition is not an argument. Nine peoples agreed, and they were wrong, and the decree they won was overturned within a reign. Numbers at the bottom of a letter establish nothing about the truth of what is written above them, and the church that remembers this will not be frightened by a consensus.

corruption_summary: Broad agreement is treated as evidence; nine peoples signed a slander that a single archive search undid.
corruption_paragraphs: The assumption that a wide consensus establishes a claim is as old as Ezra 4 and as wrong. Nine peoples put their names to a letter calling Jerusalem rebellious and bad, and the letter succeeded for a time and was false. Truth is not settled by the length of a signature list, in the fifth century BC or now.

The principle to recover is that God's cause is vindicated by God and not by the balance of opinion. The work stopped; then the LORD “turned the heart of the king” (Ezra 6:22) and the house was finished with the treasury's money and the feast kept with joy. A Christian facing a united opposition should notice how little the unanimity finally weighed.
